prompt.context: Our client is a private equity firm focused on the transportation industry. They are looking at investing in a start-up low cost airline carrier focused on the route from New York to London. Specifically they are looking to play on JetBlue's presence at JFK and EasyJet's presence at Stansted. Currently there are only large players in the market — no low cost carriers on that route.
prompt.question: Should the private equity firm invest in this start-up low cost airline?

clarifying_info.q: How many flights operate daily between New York and London?
How many seats does each plane carry, and what is the average load factor?
clarifying_info.a: 300 seats per flight; flights are 90% full on average.

clarifying_info.q: What share of passengers are price-sensitive?
What are the costs per ticket for an airline on this route?
clarifying_info.a: Plane cost $180, fuel $180, labor $60, other $60 — total $480 per ticket. This is the same for all players in the market.

clarifying_info.q: What do competitors currently charge per ticket?
Has the start-up made any progress securing assets?
clarifying_info.a: The start-up is in negotiations to procure a plane and has already negotiated terminal space at both JFK and Stansted.

exhibits.title: Example Dialogue — Candidate-Interviewer Exchange
exhibits.shows: A sample dialogue illustrating how an interviewer and candidate might work through the market-sizing and cost analysis portions of the case
exhibits.data: Market size walk-through: 40 flights x 300 seats x 90% = 10,800 passengers/day; 70% price-sensitive = 7,700 target passengers/day

framework: Market sizing — estimate total daily passenger volume on NY-London route and isolate the price-sensitive segment
Competitive landscape — identify current players, their pricing, and cost structure
Cost analysis — build up per-ticket cost for the new entrant and compare to competitor pricing
Profitability assessment — determine whether the start-up can price competitively and earn a margin
Strategic risk — evaluate competitor response (price war), start-up's ability to sustain losses, and PE exit dynamics
Recommendation — synthesize profitability, risk, and PE objectives to advise invest or not invest

questions.prompt: Size the daily market for passengers on the New York to London route.
questions.guidance: Candidate should estimate flights per day, seats per plane, and load factor. Strong answer gets to roughly 10,800–11,000 total daily passengers.

math.setup: Total daily passengers = flights per day × seats per flight × load factor

questions.prompt: How large is the addressable (price-sensitive) market for the low-cost carrier?
questions.guidance: Apply the 70% price-sensitive share to the total market.

math.setup: Addressable market = total daily passengers × price-sensitive share

questions.prompt: What is the total cost per ticket for the new low-cost carrier, and how does it compare to competitor pricing?
questions.guidance: Candidate should sum the four cost buckets and compare to the $450 competitor price. A strong candidate immediately recognises competitors are pricing below cost.

math.setup: Total cost per ticket = plane cost + fuel cost + labor cost + other costs
steps: Loss per ticket at competitor price = $450 − $480 = −$30
math.answer: $480 per ticket; competitors are selling at a $30 per-ticket loss

questions.prompt: If the start-up could reduce its costs to $350 per ticket, would you recommend entering the market?
questions.guidance: Candidate should not jump to 'yes' just because there is a positive margin at $350. Strong answer identifies the threat of a price war — established carriers are diversified and have brand equity, so they can afford to match or undercut pricing on this single route to defend it. The start-up cannot sustain a prolonged price war.

math.setup: Margin at reduced cost: price to undercut $450 minus new cost $350
steps: If new entrant prices at, say, $400 (undercutting $450): margin = $400 − $350 = $50 per ticket
But if incumbents retaliate and drop to $350 or below, new entrant margin disappears
math.answer: Even with $350 cost base, margin is fragile; price-war risk is the decisive factor

brainstorming.prompt: Why might large incumbent airlines be selling tickets below their fully-loaded cost of $480?

categories.name: Network cross-subsidisation
ideas: Diversified route network allows profits on short-haul routes to subsidise trans-Atlantic losses
NY-London route acts as a prestige/flagship route worth running at a loss for brand reasons

categories.name: Revenue management / yield mix
ideas: Business-class and premium economy tickets carry far higher margins and offset economy losses
Last-minute and peak-period bookings are priced at a large premium, raising average ticket revenue above the $450 headline figure
Ancillary revenues (cargo, loyalty program, co-branded credit cards) supplement ticket revenue

categories.name: Cost structure differences
ideas: Legacy carriers may have legacy labour agreements or older aircraft that the $480 figure doesn't fully capture, or conversely may have negotiated lower fuel hedges
Incumbents may amortise fixed assets differently, distorting per-ticket cost comparisons

recommendation: Do not recommend investing in the start-up low-cost airline on the NY-London route
The current market cost per ticket ($480) already exceeds competitor pricing ($450), meaning incumbents operate this route at a loss — likely cross-subsidised by other routes
Even if the start-up can achieve a lower cost base (~$350), a price war with better-capitalised, diversified incumbents would eliminate any margin advantage

From a PE perspective, high start-up costs, thin/negative unit economics at current market prices, and risk of a price war create an unfavourable risk/return profile for a fund looking to enter and exit within a typical PE horizon
risks: Incumbent retaliation — large carriers can price down on this single route indefinitely given diversified revenue
High capital intensity — aircraft procurement and terminal agreements require significant upfront investment before any revenue is generated
Demand uncertainty — the 70% price-sensitive share is an estimate; actual conversion rate may be lower
Regulatory and operational risk — securing landing slots, safety certification, and crew logistics for a trans-Atlantic start-up is complex
next_steps: Investigate whether the start-up has proprietary cost advantages (e.g., newer, more fuel-efficient aircraft) that could durably keep costs below $350
Analyse incumbent revenue mix more carefully to determine whether the $450 average ticket truly reflects a loss or whether yield management means average realised revenue is higher
Explore alternative investment opportunities in the low-cost carrier space on routes where incumbents are not entrenched or where cost parity is more achievable
